transcriptText:
really appreciate having the chance to
be here with you today and to talk about
how spaceports can enable the space
economy.
But first, let's have just a little bit
of history and background to put things
into context.
So, ever since the Soviet Union launched
your Gagarin into space more than 60
years ago,
almost all of the significant
achievements and historic milestones
that we've seen in space have been done
by governments.
Whether we're talking about the X-15
program, Project Mercury, Project
Gemini, the Apollo moon landings, 30
years of flying the space shuttle, or
building and living and working on board
the International Space Station,
it's been governments that have been
responsible for planning, developing,
and carrying out those programs.
going forward that is not necessarily
going to be the case because private
industry is playing an increasingly
important role.
Now there are a number of reasons for
that including things like lower costs,
increased innovation,
a greater risk tolerance,
the opportunity for new products,
services, and customers. That's not the
government's job, but it's what business
is all about. and new sources of funding
and investment so that we don't have to
rely just on congressional
appropriations and using tax dollars in
order to fund our space activities.
So, how is this new paradigm going?
Well, let's take a look at a few
metrics. All in all, I think things are
going very well. This is a plot of the
number of FAA licensed commercial
launches that are taking place every
year. And as you can see, over the last
eight years, the number has increased
exponentially,
199 last year, and there's no sign of
that turning around or even leveling
off.
How about US human space flights since
July of 2021? Well, for government
customers,
after last Friday's launch, there have
now been 11 flights for government
customers, carrying a total of 40
government astronauts to and from the
International Space Station.
10 of those flights were by SpaceX, one
by Boeing. That's great. But during that
same time period, there have been 33
flights for non-government customers
carrying 180 non-government astronauts
to space with flights like Inspiration
4, Polaris Dawn and Prom 2, four flights
for Axiom customers,
nine flights for Virgin Galactic
customers, and 17 flights for Blue
Origin customers.
We're also seeing a change in who gets
to go to space.
Wally Funk flew on the Blue Origin New
Shepard rocket at age 82, making her the
oldest person ever to go to space, but
her record only lasted a few months
because short time later, William
Shatner, you know, as Captain Kirk from
Star Trek, flew at age 90.
Haley Arseno is a childhood cancer
survivor and she flew on Inspiration 4.
John Goodwin
had previously been diagnosed with
Parkinson's and yet he flew with Virgin
Galactic.
And just last month we saw Mishi Benthos
become the first wheelchair user to go
to space.
None of those people would have had a
chance to fly as a NASA astronaut. And
yet, I think they are much more
representative of what we're going to
see in the future on commercial space
flights in terms of people that are
going to space to live, to work, or just
to visit.
Let's take a look at spaceports.
Right now, there are 14 FAA licensed
spaceports. Those are the ones shown in
blue on this map.
There's also another 15 sites on the
left hand side here.
that have either submitted their
applications or announced their
intention to apply at some point in the
future. We've also got a number of
government-owned and operated facilities
shown in red and a handful of privately
owned sites shown in black.
But of course, there's interest in space
for space not just in the United States
but all over the world.
Bryce puts together a map every year
that shows all the current and proposed
spaceports.
And as you can see, their latest edition
shows more than a hundred sites.
How about the global space economy?
Well, the Space Foundation estimates
that we're now in excess of $600 billion
dollars every year.
But what's important and significant to
me is not just the number, but who's
providing those funds. And what you can
see from the pie chart is that less than
a quarter, just the slices in orange and
gray, that's the government spending.
More than three4s of the total,
the blue and the green, is commercial
companies or private consumers.
And what's even more exciting is that if
you talk to knowledgeable economists and
financial experts, there is a very
strong consensus that that global space
economy is going to exceed $1 trillion
per year in just the next few years.
I believe that much of that economic
growth could take place at or near
spaceports.
Now, why do I say that? Well, it's based
on a new understanding of really what a
spaceport is all about. I believe that
it's not just a place from which to
launch rockets, but it can also be a
focal point or a technology hub to
enable the creation of an overarching
economic ecosystem for space related
activities.
So, what can you do at a spaceport?
There's lots of things you can launch
satellites. We're going to continue to
do that. Space tourism. We've got three
US companies that have taken dozens of
people paying their own way.
Aerospace manufacturing. This is a
picture of the Blue Origin factory just
outside the gate at the Kennedy Space
Center.
Research and technology development.
Education and training. You don't
necessarily have to be a government
employee or a NASA astronaut to do these
things anymore. NASTAR located in
Philadelphia has a centrifuge. They will
spin you around so you can experience
what it feels like to have 3Gs, 4Gs,
5Gs, or more simulating what you'll
experience if you go to space. There's
also companies like Zerog that will take
you on parabolic aircraft flights that
will allow you to experience
weightlessness for 20 seconds at a time.
So you can have that experience.
You can go through the altitude chamber.
So you can understand what the flight
attendants mean when they say in the
event of a sudden change in atmospheric
pressure. You can see what it's like to
not have sufficient oxygen to experience
hypoxia. So you can understand your own
personal symptoms and be better prepared
for a space flight. Other companies will
let you try on a space suit and see what
a spacew walk would be like.
There's also workforce development
opportunities, partnerships with all
kinds of schools
for projects, programs, internships,
co-ops, apprenticeships.
And then there's pointto-point
transportation, which is right around
the corner, and it's something that I'm
very passionate about.
What I'm talking about is the ability to
fly from one point on the Earth to the
opposite side of the planet in just an
hour or two. I think that's going to be
a major gamecher both for national
security and for economic
competitiveness.
To emphasize the point about the
technology,
a perfect example is SpaceX's Starship.
Elon Musk envisioned that vehicle as
being something to help us colonize Mars
or to help take NASA astronauts down to
the surface of the moon and back up to
lunar orbit as part of the Aremis
program. But that same system once it's
completed its test and development
program will be able to be used for
point-to-point missions
and then it's able to reach most places
on the earth in half an hour, any place
on the earth in less than an hour. It's
a huge vehicle. It has greater
pressurized volume than an Airbus 380
jumbo jet and that means it can carry
several hundred passengers or 100 metric
tons of cargo.
Now, that's a big rocket and it probably
not practical to be able to fly that too
close to densely populated areas. But
there's a dozen other companies that are
working on other systems, a little
smaller with slightly less capability,
but still designed for that
point-to-point mission. Some of those
are horizontal takeoff and landing, some
vertical takeoff and landing. And it's
not just in the United States. There's
other countries working on this, too.
Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany,
and Canada among others.
[snorts]
Now, I'm really surprised given how
important and significant that type of
capability is that we're not hearing
more discussion about that in public.
Now the military has shown some interest
in terms of what could you do with that
in the event of a natural disaster or a
humanitarian crisis med medical
emergency or in the event of actual or
anticipated military action somewhere.
But if we just use this for military
purposes we are missing out.
I think the economic potential is huge.
One of my favorite statistics is that
every year more than 150 million people
fly on an airplane for more than 10
hours on their flight.
If you could convince 5% of that total
to consider flying in a space fly space
plane of one sort or another, and let's
just say what if the ticket costs
$2,500.
It's probably going to be more than
that. But if it were only $2,500, that
would mean $20 billion in revenues for
this type of market. That dwarfs what
we're currently spending on rockets to
la on satellites into orbit. So the
potential is huge.
Now NASA has done studies where they've
gotten some teams surveying folks and
asking them how much would you pay to
deliver a package in 12 hours? How about
10 hours? How about eight hours? How
about four hours? And the same thing for
taking people from one point to another.
And what they found out is there's a
tremendous market out there. There's
dozens of flights that would be
profitable. you could close the business
case for an appropriately sized vehicle.
So, let's wrap up by taking a look at
some specific examples or or case
studies, if you will, of what an a
spaceport could do that might be of
interest. There's a company called Dawn
Aerospace that has built a small
unmanned rocket powered space plane that
they're flying from New Zealand
and it's already flown more than 50
flights. It's broken the sound barrier.
It set a new time to climb record that
previously was owned by the anup F-15
fighter
and it's gone more than 82,000 ft. It's
designed to be able to reach the edge of
space at a 100 kilometer altitude on a
suborbital flight, taking off from a
runway and then coming back and landing
on a runway.
They're intending this to be able to fly
a 100 times a year, twice a day if you
need it. And that kind of capability at
a much lower cost than we're currently
spending is so impressive that the state
of Oklahoma has now reached out and
signed a contract to buy one of those
systems. So, at the beginning of next
year,
Dawn Aerospace is going to deliver the
state of Oklahoma their own space plane
that they can fly from the Oklahoma
Spaceport. They've never had a launch
before. And right away, they're going to
be one of the most active spaceports in
the world with something going to the
edge of space a 100 times or more per
year.
Well, what if you don't have a runway?
You can talk to other companies like New
Frontier Aerospace. They're building a
vertical takeoff and landing system. Not
designed to launch satellites, but for
this point-to-point mission
can fly Mach 8 at 150,000 ft. So, it's
so high you wouldn't even hear the sonic
boom on the ground. And then finally,
Houston Spaceport.
This is one of the most successful
spaceports in the world. And yet they've
never had a launch.
They have decided they want to be a
strategic
intermodal transportation hub. And in
the meantime, they've built partnerships
with the government, with academia, and
with industry. You can see some of their
tenants that you recognize. Companies
that build space suits, space stations,
robotic lunar landers, avionics, and
hypersonic space planes.
And the result has been billions of
dollars in contracts,
multi- hundreds of millions of dollars
in construction projects, and thousands
of new jobs. So the community loves that
spaceport. So bottom line, spaceports
can be a tremendous enabler for economic
growth, and I think every state should
have at least one.
If you have any questions or would like
some more information, feel free to
reach out to me, LinkedIn or email.
Happy to chat with you further. Thank
you very much.
